comment: MiniDAQ's threat model (Chapter 17): the elements of the data flow diagram (dataflow.dot) and a STRIDE analysis of each. tools/check_threats.py (test docs.threats) checks that every element has a threat or a reason for every STRIDE category that applies to its kind, that a mitigated threat names requirements that exist and are verified, and that the risk controls it names exist. Prose, assumptions and the attack tree: threat-model.md.

stride.S: Spoofing: pretending to be someone or something else
stride.R: Repudiation: denying an action, for lack of evidence
stride.I: Information disclosure: exposing data to someone not allowed to see it
stride.D: Denial of service: making the service unavailable or degraded
stride.E: Elevation of privilege: doing what one's role does not allow

elements.name: Control client: minidaq_ctl, a GUI, a script
minidaq_server: control server and acquisition service
Token file, start-up token, TLS private key
Crash report file (--crash-report), or the service manager's journal

threats.threat: A process on the acquisition PC or the network connects to the control port and sends stop or configure as if it were the operator's console (hazard H-08).
A dashboard that holds an observer token is used to stop a scan.
An operator denies having stopped or reconfigured a scan.
threats.note: The audit trail records the token's name and the client's address for every command; a shared token makes the name a group, not a person (assumption: confirm with team whether operators get personal tokens).

threats.threat: A device on the detector link sends MDQ-R1 packets as if it were a readout board, and its words are acquired as data.
threats.note: The readout protocol has no authentication: the link is point to point or on the scanner's own network (threat-model.md, section 6). Packets with another source id or a wrong format are counted and rejected, and the counters reach the integrity verdict.

threats.threat: A readout board denies having sent its data.
threats.note: A readout board performs no action that a person could deny; each packet states the source id of its board.

threats.threat: A program listens on the control port before minidaq_server does, or in its place, and collects the tokens that clients send.
threats.note: Over TLS the client sends a token only to a server whose certificate it verified. On loopback without TLS, a process of another user that binds the port first can collect the start-up token: TLS on loopback is the remedy where the PC has several users (threat-model.md, section 6).

threats.threat: The minidaq_server binary or its libraries on the acquisition PC are replaced.
threats.note: Integrity of installed software is the platform's (signed packages, Chapter 25); MiniDAQ's part is the SBOM that says what should be installed.

threats.threat: The server's own decisions (a fault, a refused command, a closed connection) leave no record.
The status and the diagnostics response, readable by observers, show file paths, the configuration and the recent events of the flight recorder; an error message shows internals.
threats.note: The status and the diagnostics hold no patient data (MiniDAQ holds no patient identity, Chapter 12) and no secret: a diagnostics event is a code and two numbers, and a test checks the response's fields (SRS-DIAG-004, Chapter 21). An observer is a trusted role. Responses never echo a token.

threats.threat: Clients that connect and say nothing hold all eight client slots, so the operator's console cannot connect.
A client sends an endless request line or malformed JSON to exhaust memory or crash the server.
threats.note: The 64 KiB limit, a test that sends every field of a request with every JSON type, and the protocol fuzz target (fuzz_protocol), which also checks that no command succeeds without its role. The fuzz target found an auth token of the wrong type that ended the server (MDQ-PR-013).

threats.threat: A defect in the protocol lets a client run a command its role does not allow, for example a command added later without a role.
threats.note: required_role() gives every command that it does not know the operator role; the fuzz target checks the property.

threats.threat: A machine between client and server changes a command in transit, for example the configuration's coincidence window.
An eavesdropper on the network reads a token and replays it.
A flood of connections or TLS handshakes from the network keeps the server's one thread busy.
threats.note: Rate limiting belongs to the network (the scanner's network is not open to the site); the server closes connections that do not finish in time and the acquisition threads do not depend on the control thread.

threats.threat: Packets are changed in transit on the detector link.
threats.note: Format checks catch random corruption, not a deliberate change; the link is physically controlled.

threats.threat: The detector data is read on the link.
threats.note: Detector words carry no patient identity; the link is physically controlled.

threats.threat: A flood of datagrams on the detector port makes the receiver drop real packets.
threats.note: Losses are counted and make the run incomplete (H-01's controls): the scan is not silently wrong, and the environment keeps the link closed.

threats.threat: A configuration file is changed so that a scan runs with other settings.
threats.note: Configuring needs an operator token; the effective configuration is recorded with the data, so a change is visible.

threats.threat: Nobody can tell which configuration a run used.
Configuration files are read by another user.
threats.note: They hold settings, no secrets: tokens and keys are never part of a configuration.

threats.threat: A configuration file is deleted or made invalid before a scan.
threats.note: An invalid configuration is rejected with every error at once, before the run, which is a delay, not a wrong scan.

threats.threat: Someone adds their own token, with the operator role, to the token file.
Someone denies having changed the token file.
threats.note: The token files record no actions; a change to them is an administrator's action on the PC, recorded by the site's own controls if at all.

threats.threat: The start-up token, a client's token file or the TLS private key is read by another user of the PC, or found in a backup or a log.
threats.note: The start-up token is readable only by its owner (SRS-SEC-009), minidaq_ctl refuses a token file that others can read, the server stores only hashes and the audit trail never holds a token. Protecting the TLS private key and the clients' files is the site's (RC-25). Tokens start with mdq_ so that secret scanners can recognize a leaked one.

threats.threat: The token file is deleted or damaged, so the server does not start or nobody can authenticate.
threats.note: The server refuses to start with a message; the remedy is a new token, which is an administrator's task.

threats.threat: List-mode files are changed after the run.
threats.note: Every block carries a CRC-32, which detects damage but not a deliberate change with a recomputed CRC: signing the run's files is a recorded gap (threat-model.md, section 7).

threats.threat: Nobody can tell which run produced a file, or under which settings.
The data of a scan is read by someone who may not see it.
threats.note: The files carry no patient identity; the link to a patient is made by the scanner's software, whose storage is protected by the site.

threats.threat: The disk is filled, so that a run cannot be stored.
threats.note: A write failure is a fault that the operator sees, not a silent loss. Preventing another user from filling the disk is the site's (threat-model.md, section 6, item 8; gap in section 7).

threats.threat: Entries are removed from the audit trail or changed to hide an action.
threats.note: The trail is appended, never rewritten, and flushed per record; protecting it from its own user (forwarding to a log server, a hash chain) is a recorded gap (threat-model.md, section 7).

threats.threat: An action is denied for lack of a record in the audit trail.
threats.note: The audit trail is the evidence against repudiation (T-03, T-08); its own integrity is T-31.

threats.threat: The audit trail exposes secrets or personal data.
threats.note: It holds token names and client addresses, never tokens.

threats.threat: The audit trail cannot be written (disk full), and actions go unrecorded.
threats.note: minidaq_server counts failed audit writes and reports them at shutdown with a non-zero exit status; stopping scans because the audit trail is full would trade a security gap for a safety one (assumption: confirm with team).

threats.threat: Someone changes a crash report, or writes a false one, to mislead the investigation of a failure.
threats.note: The file is created with mode 0600 in the operator's account (section 6, items 1 and 2). The report names the build ID, which the investigation checks against the shipped build (Chapter 21).

threats.threat: Repudiation of an action through the crash report.
threats.note: The report records the signal and the server's own recent events, not the actions of users; the audit trail does that.

threats.threat: Whoever reads the crash report learns the server's version, build ID, code addresses and recent events, which can help an attack on the server.
threats.note: The report holds no token, key or patient data. Whoever can read the operator's files is already inside the boundary of section 2, where MiniDAQ does not defend; the addresses describe one run of a randomized layout (assumption: confirm with team whether crash reports sent to the manufacturer need a data protection review).

threats.threat: The crash report cannot be written, so the evidence of a crash is lost.
threats.note: A file that cannot be opened stops the server at start, visibly. A write that fails while the process dies loses the report but not the core dump, which the system keeps (Chapter 21); the acquisition is not affected, since the process is ending anyway.
